sections.h2: What a lady bird deed is in Michigan
sections.html:
It's a deed in which the owner keeps a life estate and full power to sell, mortgage or lease the home, while naming someone who receives it at the owner's death. Michigan's Department of Health and Human Services defines it as an enhanced life estate deed, also called a transfer on death deed, that lets property pass on death without probate. The owner still owns the property and can sell, rent or change it without restriction until death.

Michigan Treasury describes nearly the same picture in its principal residence exemption guidance: an owner deeds the home to another person while reserving a life estate and full power to convey during life, including selling, gifting, mortgaging, leasing or keeping the proceeds. Treasury names that arrangement a Lady Bird Deed.

The instrument still has to be a valid Michigan deed. The statutory short form for a quitclaim makes a conveyance a good one to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns when it is worded in substance as a quitclaim and is signed, sealed and acknowledged by the grantor (MCL 565.152). That form alone doesn't describe a retained life estate, so the wording of the retained powers is what a Michigan attorney will draft.

Two separate rules are in play, and both come from the state agency. On eligibility, because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, a lady bird deed isn't considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

Estate recovery is a different question. It applies to Medicaid beneficiaries who are 55 or older and received long-term care services on or after September 30, 2007. The agency defines the estate as property passing to heirs through probate, but for someone who received an asset disregard from a long-term care partnership policy, recovery applies to all assets whether or not they pass through probate (MDHHS Estate Recovery).

Recovery is deferred while a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or permanently disabled child is living. An undue hardship waiver is possible for a home of modest value, meaning one worth less than 50% of the average home price in its county on the date of death, and the applicant must pass a means test: household income under 200% of the federal guideline and household resources under $10,000.

Transferring assets to avoid recovery can affect eligibility, and the law presumes no undue hardship when the hardship results from such a transfer (MCL 400.112g(3)(e)(iii)). Speak with a legal advisor before you sign a deed with Medicaid in mind.

sections.h2: Effect on the exemption and taxable value
sections.html:
The deed can change who qualifies for the principal residence exemption. A person who holds a life estate counts as a partial owner and is eligible if the home is their principal residence, and any ownership interest must be in writing. In the lady bird example, the person named to receive the home has no current ownership interest because the grantor keeps full control. That person becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the grantor hasn't used the powers.

Taxable value is a separate issue. Under MCL 211.27a, a transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the year after the transfer. Subsection (6) defines transfer of ownership broadly, and subsection (7) lists transfers that fall outside the definition. Whether a particular deed, or the later death of the grantor, counts is a question for the local assessor.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has a lady bird deed
sections.html:
If the deed keeps the full powers described above, the grantor is the person who sells. The owner may sell or rent without restriction until death, and the retained powers include selling, gifting, mortgaging and leasing. A buyer's title company will still want to read the recorded deed itself, because a deed written with narrower powers changes who must sign.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and read the retained powers.
  • Ask the title company whether it needs the named recipient's signature or a release.
  • If the grantor has died, the deed that names the recipient is the starting point, and the recipient should ask the assessor and the title company how the transfer is handled.

Michigan's simplified affidavit for small estates, court form PC 598, can be used only when no real property is in the decedent's estate, so a house isn't handled through that form.

A deceased owner is no longer eligible for the exemption because the owner can't occupy the home or intend to return. The estate's personal representative or trustee must file Form 2602, the Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, with the assessor within 90 days of death. The exemption is removed as of December 31 of the year the rescission was filed.

The person who receives the home and lives there can claim a new exemption by filing Form 2368 with the assessor if they meet the ownership rules, by June 1 for the summer levy or November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A property transfer affidavit may also be needed, so ask the local assessor which filings apply to a transfer at death.

The deed is a recorded legal document, and small wording differences control who owns what. Bring these questions to a Michigan attorney.

  • Which powers does the deed reserve: selling, mortgaging, leasing and gifting?
  • Does the owner want a Medicaid planning result, and how does estate recovery apply if there is a long-term care partnership policy?
  • How will the county assessor treat the deed for uncapping and the principal residence exemption?
  • Who will file the rescission and affidavit forms after death, and within what time?

Call the assessor for the city or township where the home sits, and the register of deeds for the county, for their recording and filing requirements.

sections.h2: Selling for cash with a deed already in place
sections.html:
An owner who already recorded a lady bird deed can still sell the home during life, and a cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender's underwriting. The steps are the same as any sale where the grantor signs: confirm the retained powers, order the title search, and settle any mortgage payoff at closing.

Once the sale closes, the named recipient has nothing to receive at death from that property, because the home is no longer the grantor's. If the proceeds matter for long-term care planning, talk with a legal advisor before closing, since the money, not the house, becomes the asset to plan around.

faqs.q: Does Michigan call it a lady bird deed in official materials?
faqs.a: Yes, in two places. The state Medicaid policy glossary lists Lady Bird Deed as another name for an enhanced life estate deed or transfer on death deed, and Treasury's exemption guidance uses the term in an ownership example.

faqs.q: Is a lady bird deed a Medicaid divestment in Michigan?
faqs.a: No. Because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, the deed isn't considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

faqs.q: Does the deed avoid Medicaid estate recovery?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Recovery reaches all assets, probate or not, for beneficiaries who received an asset disregard under a long-term care partnership policy, so ask a legal advisor how your facts apply.

faqs.q: Can the person named in the deed claim the principal residence exemption?
faqs.a: Not while the grantor keeps full control. That person has no current ownership interest and becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the powers were not used.

faqs.q: Does recording a lady bird deed raise property taxes?
faqs.a: That depends on whether the conveyance is a transfer of ownership under MCL 211.27a. A transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the next calendar year, so ask the local assessor before you record.
